## Operational (Main) module:

1. ### **Database:**

**![][image2]**

2. ### **Operations:**

   This is where all software operations, whether they were pos or admin-based belong. Apart from the engine’s reasoning and decisions, the retailer will have access to these features:

   **A. POS / Checkout (cashier-facing, terminal-level)**

* Scan or manually search a product to add to cart  
* Adjust quantity / remove a line item before completing sale  
* Weighted/PLU entry for scale-based items (produce, deli)  
* Apply a discount — per item or whole transaction, with a reason code. *(if this operation is done without previous decision, than it must be the Retailer/Manager only)*  
* Price override, gated behind manager PIN/role ★ ( Staff.Role \+ Code/PIN supports this) *(Retailer/Manager)*  
* Attach a customer to the transaction (loyalty lookup by phone/card)  
* Split payment across multiple tender types in one transaction  
* Process payment (cash tendered/change calc, card, mobile wallet)  
* Print or send digital receipt (SMS/email)  
* Reprint a past receipt  
* Void a line item or void the whole transaction pre-finalization  
* No-sale (open drawer without a sale — logged for accountability, common shrinkage-audit point) *(Retailer/Manager unless permission given).*  
* Park/hold a transaction and resume later  
* Return/refund at register, linked to the original transaction *(unless under a specific policy, Retailer/Manager only).*  
* Store credit *(Retailer/Manager)*  
* Cash drawer paid-in / paid-out (petty cash movements) *(Retailer/Manager)*  
* Clock in/out at the terminal ★ (feeds Shifts entity)  
* Real-time Engine notifications surfaced during checkout, permission-gated ★ *(Retailer, with pre-determined privileges to the manager/cashier )*  
* Manual stock lookup mid-sale ("is this in stock elsewhere / back room")

  **B. Shift & end-of-day reconciliation** *(Retailer)*

* X-report — read-only mid-shift snapshot  
* Z-report — end-of-day close: gross sales by tender type, transaction count, voids/no-sales, discounts/overrides applied, cash variance   
* Drawer float count at shift start, counted total at shift end, variance flagged  
* Per-cashier shift handover summary

  This category is worth taking seriously even though it looks like "just admin paperwork" — it's the main mechanism retailers use to catch internal shrinkage, and it's something checkout-only software almost always has in some form, so skipping it would be a regression versus what they're used to, not a simplification.

  **C. Product & catalog management**

* Add product/variant — manual, CSV import, or barcode-scan against a seed catalog ★*(Retailer/ Manager)*  
* Edit product/variant details *(Retailer/ Manager)*  
* Manage category hierarchy *(Retailer/ Manager)*  
* Bulk price update across a category or product line *(Retailer)*  
* Print barcode/shelf labels *(Retailer/ Manager)*  
* Discontinue/archive a product (Status field) *(Retailer)*  
* Create a bundle (link multiple products as a combo) *(Retailer)*

  **D. Inventory & stock**

* Receive a delivery against a Purchase Order (creates Batch \+ Inventory rows) *(Retailer/ Manager)*  
* Manual stock adjustment — damage, loss, correction (Stock\_movements) *(Retailer/ Manager)*  
* Physical stock count / cycle count reconciliation against system quantity *(Retailer/ Manager)*  
* View current stock by store, variant, and batch *(Retailer/ Manager)*  
* Flag near-expiry batches for markdown ★  *(Retailer)*  
* Transfer stock between stores — listed but deferred

  **E. Customer management**

* Add/edit customer profile (which includes privacy settings and information)  
* Loyalty points accrual and redemption (Not automated)  
* View a customer's purchase history *(Retailer/ Manager)*  
* Manual tier override *(Retailer/ Manager)*  
* Customer-specific discount assignment(Not automated) *(Retailer)*

  **F. Staff / shift management** *(Retailer)*

* Add/edit staff account, assign role and PIN  
* Clock in/out, basic shift scheduling  
* View sales performance per staff member ★  
* Deactivate/terminate a staff account

  **G. Supplier & purchasing**

* Add/edit supplier record and terms (Supplier-Variant) *(Retailer/ Manager)*  
* Create a Purchase Order — manually or from an Engine recommendation ★ *(Retailer/ Manager only if having recommendation permission)*  
* Track PO status (pending / partially received / received) *(Retailer/ Manager)*  
* Log delivery discrepancies (expected vs. received quantity, late arrival) *(Retailer/ Manager)*

  **H. Promotions & pricing** *(Retailer)*

* Create a promotion, scoped to product or specific variant, with validity window  
* Activate/deactivate/schedule a promotion  
* Price history tracking (already supported structurally by Price entity) ★

  **I. Returns & refunds (admin-side)**

* Review/approve returns above a policy threshold  
* Return-reason analytics *(Retailer/ Manager)*

  **J. Store & system administration** *(Retailer)*

* Manage store profile (hours, address, manager)  
* Manage terminals per store  
* Multi-store viewing for a retailer with more than one location (viewing only — the transfer workflow itself stays deferred)  
* User role/permission management

  **K. Engine interaction** ★ — this whole category has no equivalent in checkout-only software, worth presenting to retailers as the headline difference. *(Retailer)*

* View the recommendation feed, grouped by department  
* Accept or decline a recommendation — accepting triggers the real downstream action (e.g., accepted reorder → creates a Purchase Order)  
* View the explanation behind a recommendation  
* Dismiss or snooze a notification

  **L. Social/e-commerce flagging** ★

* Flag an order as sourced from a social channel.  
* Basic tracking of social-sourced order volume *(Retailer/ Manager).*

## Statistics module:

So Statistics basically is being fed from the operational module, every decision made by the retailer/ the engine or a transaction is added to this module. This module also provides *pseudonymization ,* through 3 tiers:  
**Tier 1 (raw events)** — holds real identifiers. Local, never syncs.  
**Tier 2 (computed cache)** — pseudonymization happens here. This is the boundary.  
**Tier 3 (consumption)** — the engine sees pseudonymous keys only.  
**The pseudonym** is `HMAC-SHA256(tenant_key, "waymark:customer:v1:" ‖ customer_id)`, truncated to 128 bits. There is no mapping table: what is kept separately is the **key**, which never leaves the premises and is in no backup and no sync payload *(revised 11/09/2026 — see decisions.md D-039)*.   
 Below a list of like 30 stats \-to be presented with graphs-, only like 4 show to the dashboard (i.e Revenue, most sold products, …) this module provides all needed data for the Engine to operate in an organized manner.  *Here is a suggested list :*

3. New customer acquisition

     (*Net sales by product / category / store / period, after returns/discounts*)

## Analytical Engine:

This is the most important part, the engine is able to do a lot of operations (among are listed below) it has a specific section when the retailer can get the data along with what the engine has analyzed in each section \+ tiles in the main dashboard for important notes (Product A is underperforming suggested to lower its orders) \+ real-time notifications (Product B is purchased \=\> the engine calculated that’s the reorder point \=\> Suggests ordering) in these 2 features the retailer can click to move to detailed report and decision analysis, Some features:

1) **Inventory Department:** The department is divided into stages:

   We start with real-time monitoring which Continuously tracks:

* current stock  
* stock value  
* incoming stock  
* outgoing stock  
* damaged/lost stock  
* adjustments  
* days of inventory remaining


  We then discuss deciding on inventory:

  **Group 1 — Stock Health Monitoring**

* Current stock & value, by variant/store/batch — direct read from Inventory table  
* Incoming stock — from open Purchase Orders not yet received  
* Days of inventory remaining — this is the one prediction in this group, needs Sales' demand rate  
* Damaged/lost/adjustment feed — straight from Stock\_movements

  **Group 2 — Replenishment (Ordering)**

* Reorder point calculation  
* Safety stock calculation  
* Recommended order quantity  
* Reorder timing  
* Expected stockout date  
   → Accept creates a Purchase Order, which is where this department hands off to Supply for the actual supplier selection.

  **Group 3 — Risk & Waste Management** 

* Overstock detection  
* Dead stock / slow movers  
* Declining products (consumes Sales & Demand's trend output)  
* Expiration detection on near-expiry batches  
   → This belongs in "movements/reports" rather than "ordering" since it's not about placing an order. It operates:

  **Near-Expiry Clearance Strategy:** Evaluates sequential 3-stage markdown decisions for expiring batches, outputting the exact discount path that maximizes expected recovery value. 

  **An architecture nuance this split surfaces**

  Group 2's accept/decline is binary — approve the order or don't. But Group 3's recommendations. That means the Integration Layer's shared recommendation contract needs to support "pick one of several suggested actions, or dismiss." 

2) **Sales & Demand Department:**The department is divided into:

   Forecasting demand by product, category ..  which is done in a rolling fashion (updated each time), doing variance analysis to explain non-accurate forecasts.

    We also check for anomalies and try to explain them.

   Analyzing product performance is of a big importance, we observe growth, decline, sales contribution, margin, turnover,

   demand trend, customer penetration. And generate conclusions from them.

3) **Customer Department:** We start by segmentation by:

   RFM, purchase frequency, spending, categories,

   basket composition, recency.

   We also deal with *Churn / inactivity detection* and *Customer lifetime value*. Then we will generate personalized recommendations to improve loyalty and solve issues, some examples of this include the system suggesting special bundles or promotions for that specific customer on some products, if the approval arrives then the recommendations will show at checkout, for security reasons we must respect this:

   Segment on non-sensitive categories only

- Credit and tier decisions stay **informational, never actionable** — no accept/decline loop.   
- All customer-facing output routes through retailer approval  
4) **Planning Department:** This is one of the most advanced ones, if the retailer is willing to plan for management decisions, he consults this dep, it provides:

    **1\. Order Planning (budget-constrained optimization)**

   *"I have this much budget — what should I order across my product mix to maximize profit?"*

   Given budget, demand forecast (Sales), cost/price (Supply), and expiration limits (Inventory), output a suggested order plan

   **2\. Promotion & Price Sensitivity Sandbox:** Allows the retailer to slider-adjust advertising spend or discount rates to visualize best-case, worst-case, and expected net profit before launching a campaign.

   **3\. New Product EVSI Pilot Tester:** Evaluates whether to order a new product store-wide, skip it, or run a 2-week pilot order to test demand. Calculates the Expected Value of Sample Information (EVSI) dynamically. 

   **4\. Risk & Cash Flow Simulator:** Simulates 1,000 potential future months to show the retailer their full probability distribution of stockouts, holding costs, and profit margin, monthly or triggered on-demand before a big purchasing decision

   **5\. Knapsack / MIP Order Allocation:** Solves a Mixed-Integer Program that scales back reorder quantities when total recommended purchasing costs exceed the retailer's monthly budget or total store shelf volume.

   **6\. Multi-Period Order Batcher:** Uses the Wagner-Whitin algorithm to group future projected demand into optimal delivery batches, preventing unnecessary fixed truck delivery fees, only for non-perishable products.

5) **Supply Department:** So we start by tracking the following variables:

   

* average lead time  
* lead-time variability  
* on-time delivery  
* fulfillment rate  
* quantity discrepancies  
* purchase price  
* price evolution  
* product availability


  Which will enable analyzing: *Supplier recommendation, comparison and risk*

  **Supplier Selection under Risk:** Evaluates competing vendors when a primary supplier has lead-time uncertainty or price variations. It operates by watching what suppliers a retailer actually picks over time — A real behavioral datato *infer* an implicit risk-aversion parameter instead of asking for one directly. 

Here is a table which present the format of operation of each department:

| Point/ Department | Input | Trigger timing | Output shape | Decision/ feedback loop | Cold start feedback |
| :---: | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| **Inventory** | All stats related to inventory \+ some forecasts from the insights part for estimating needed variables. | It’s triggered at transactions, on a daily/weekly basis according to the option provided. | Detailed reports at each group, also recommendations to order, solve issues .. according to the group. | Same mechanism as Supply's revealed-preference learning. Concretely: if a retailer repeatedly orders less than Group 2 recommends, that's a signal to soften the safety-stock margin over time. If they repeatedly ignore a Group 3 near-expiry flag on a category, that's a signal that the category's markdown threshold is off. Same learning pattern, applied to two different parameter sets. | Group 1 works from day one, no history needed. Group 2 is hard without history — reorder point and safety stock are statistical formulas built on demand variance and lead-time variance. We will fall back to simple deterministic thresholds;  Group 3 — overstock/dead-stock/declining-trend detection also needs history by definition (you can't detect a decline without a trend), which aren't available at cold start,  Expiration detection: it only needs the date, which is known the moment a delivery is logged — zero sales history required. Works from day one.  |
| **Sales & Demand** | all stats related to profit, reversal and product classification and customers data (In general not by customer), stats related to orders, transactions, and product performance as well. | It’s triggered on a daily basis since it’s deeply regression and forecasting with conclusion so there’s no need to call it at each time. | Generally as a dedicated section, where the retailer checks daily/weekly the performance of the business and is helped in taking decisions regarding that. Which are of the form: we need to focus more on this product, customers, category with explanation, the results are also given at recommendation level LATER in orders or such things. | outside recommendations, the results are only shown, it’s the retailer who decides whether to follow or not, | We will rely on simple heuristics as always, things that are deterministic in some sense and not risking completely inaccurate forecasts until the beta is done. |
| **Customer** | 1-7, 13, 24, all stats related to customers. | It’s triggered at transactions, on a daily/weekly basis according to the stat | Some recommendations at checkout, which include special promotions or bundles that are created which maximize his loyalty. also in its dedicated space to study options to increase loyalty of best/most customers.. | Nothing important, the system continues its work in giving insights. | For this there are plenty of static operations that serve this department without data needed, we’ll rely on them. |
| **Planning** | Depends on the service, but most need history of prices, demand forecasts, inventory group 2 output .. | Mostly on demand for all services, unless the retailer asks for one before a major decision. | Each service’s output is highlighted in its definition. | In the form of reports/ orders while the retailer’s decision is also taken into consideration for future services. | Most services either require prior sales or other departments’ output so the options are either disabled or powered by simple equivalents or estimates. |
| **Supply** | Supplier performance (Revenue, units, margin and product contribution by supplier, lead time distribution, delivery performance, availability) \+ insights related to these quantities computed by our forecasting tool. | Sorting suppliers when an order is to be created is a direct call to this department, there will also be a section of suppliers dedicated to showing the insights we talked about \+ some simple reports. | The first 2 use cases are the ones we talked about previously, the insights (forecasts) are to be used in other departments, i.e. lead-time in inventory. | In addition to the consequences of the action, like creating the orders, updating suppliers stats like, last use, number of uses .. we will observe patterns in the retailer preferences (ignoring insights and keeping one supplier ..) and add it as a decision metric in the selection for next times. | Most probably no choice, just listing suppliers, unless there’s a difference in clear attributes like price. |

- **Integration Layer:** this layer is responsible of monitoring all departments and managing outputs, displaying them with explanations and reports and also doing actions:

  When any of the previously mentioned departments have a request to output some information, like a recommendation or a notification of some reports it’s issued to this layer which checks roles and decides on whether it’s able to send the notification, if that’s not the case, it stores it \-along with previous ones not sent yet- in a dedicated section where we’ll be able to show them all to the one with privileges once he logs in. In the other case where a notification is reviewed and a decision is made, the layer takes this decision to the stats module (for future related insights) and takes an action \-the case of approval- editing on our main DB with source attribute carried from the issuing department.

   Concerning recommendation shape it actually depends on the request sent by the department and the layer just places the meta-data (something like : {department, explanation/view-more report, urgency, action\_type: binary | menu, options\[\], source}. ) in a format.

  From a security perspective, this layer does the following:

  First half (Cloud side):

- Engine emits recommendations keyed by pseudonym.

  Second half (Store side):

- The Layer resolves to a real customer only at delivery to POS or Admin  
- Every resolution writes to `processing_log` — respecting "who consulted or disclosed"  
- Before delivering any customer-directed recommendation, check `objection_flag`


**Consolidated cold-start reference**

| Parameter | Default | Used by |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Stockout rate baseline | 8-12% | Inventory Group 2, Risk Simulator |
| Overall shrinkage | 2-3% of revenue | Risk Simulator |
| Perishable-category waste | 4-8% (varies by category) | Inventory Group 3 |
| Safety stock service level | 90% blended, ABC-tiered when available (A:95%+, B:80-90%, C:70-80%) | Inventory Group 2 |
| Z-score lookup | 1.28 (90%) / 1.65 (95%) / 2.33 (99%) | Inventory Group 2 |
| Near-expiry markdown path | 20-25% / 40-50% / 60-70% | Near-Expiry Clearance |
| Lead-time uncertainty | Wide/conservative until \~5+ POs completed | Supply, EVSI, Safety stock |
| Supplier ranking weight | 50/50 price/reliability until revealed-preference data exists | Supplier Selection |

# Product Info:

* Migration, which is one of the highest challenges in a risk averse population we’re planning to implement a set of options such as copying data from the past software, and others mentioned previously, also one of the important stuff is a beta version that goes up to 3 months, with no required subscription which will bring many customers, help us collect data and develop the product (the choice of duration also helps with forecasting season), and make them relying on the software and eventually buying it.  
* For pricing the decision hasn't been made yet. It's a difficult one because evaluating this software, it should be high where the customers are sensitive to that where they used to buy one-time cheap ones so it’s to be decided later.  
* For identity, we decided on the name (“Waymark”) and all design info is on the file: [Waymark\_Brand\_Identity](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1DO4HqqZ0IBA-Wlgite5cvSwU4plckXu02qJ60rW-VcY/edit?usp=sharing). I’m also thinking of making the engine its own brand which will give it much more fame and interest, something like smartR v1 or so.

* ### **Data placement**

  **Local (store):**  
* Full operational DB — products, prices, inventory, batches, open transactions. The POS must keep selling when the line drops.  
* `Customers` direct identifiers: name, phone, email, address  
* `Staff` identifiers  
* The tenant key that makes a pseudonym — never backed up to the cloud, never synced (D-039)  
* Consent records and notice versions  
  **Cloud (Algeria):**  
* Statistics tiers 2 and 3 — pseudonymized  
* Transaction history keyed by pseudonym  
* Products, batches, suppliers, purchase orders — no personal data  
* The engine, all five departments  
* Backups  
  **The boundary is Statistics tier 1 → tier 2\.** Pseudonymization happens on the way out of the store. Nothing carrying a direct identifier crosses it.  
* To support global market, we need Deployment per jurisdiction , and some regulations need to be respected:  
* No hardcoded region or residency assumptions anywhere  
* Retention periods as config, not constants  
* Consent notice text and versioning as data — we'll need different texts per jurisdiction, and we already need versioning for Article 9(b)  
* Legal basis as a field, because GDPR's legitimate interest is far more usable than Algeria's consent-heavy regime, and it may used in the EU  
* No cross-region data paths, even for analytics  
* The payment provider is a plug-in behind an interface. Waymark owns subscription state, entitlements and invoice records itself; no provider's data model leaks into the product.

  # Apps info:

  So the software is basically divided into 2 apps. **POS** app which runs on every checkout place, it’s responsible for doing pos services, the cashier can log-in according to his privileges, all data are saved into the statistics module, the engine is then triggered \-since it only sees stats- if he has any important notifications he will show them \-only if the cashier signed in has the right to do the move- or rather store them where they belong where the retailer will take a look at later.

  Now for orders, as we agreed we will have a section for suppliers, supply will be done either by a recommendation or through its specified section, when new items arrive they’re scanned and added as New Product in Products section.

  The second app is for the **Admin**, this is where the retailer has access to all info, he can access through his dashboard what relates to customers, stuff, products, discounts, orders …, he will also be able to see the analytics section which shows the important stats with some simple insights, and most importantly the engine’s departments where he accesses reports, insights and recommendations and decides on what to accept or decline. *See a representation of the software operation:*
